newsitem.title: INDIA: India report pinpoints bungling in arms drop case.
newsitem.headline: India report pinpoints bungling in arms drop case.

text.p: A parliamentary committee has accused the Indian government of a "total security foul-up" that allowed a foreign plane to drop a huge cache of arms and let the prime suspect dash to safety.
The biting report alleged major lapses on the part of three ministries in detecting and responding to the arms drop of December 17, 1995 in the eastern state of West Bengal.

After the night-time air drop, authorities recovered 241 AK-47 and AK-56 assault rifles with more than 24,000 rounds of ammunition, 77 anti-tank grenades, 10 rocket launchers and 11 9mm pistols, according to the 51-page report.
The government has said the weapons were destined for the Hindu religious cult Ananda Marg, which has its headquarters near the site of the drop in Purulia district.

"The Committee has found alarming shortcomings in the functioning of these governmental agencies in respect of sharing of important intelligence information, operations of unscheduled aircraft in the Indian skies, radar surveillance and, above all, inter-departmental coordination," the report, dated May 7, said.

The report, based on testimony by the ministries of home (interior), defence and civil aviation, pinpointed a string of administrative blunders that enabled the Russian-built AN-26 plane to re-enter Indian airspace four days after the drop.

Former British army officer Peter Bleach and five Latvians were arrested five days after the parachute drop when Indian Air Force jets forced the plane to land in Bombay. They are among 14 people who were indicted and face trial for sedition.
But the plane's co-pilot, identified by Indian authorities as a New Zealander named Kim Davy, was not picked up by airport officials after the aircraft landed in Bombay.

"No security man was found anywhere around at the time of the landing of the aircraft. A jeep came in and Mr Kim P. Davy got into it and disappeared," the report said, adding that the home secretary had conceded "there was total security foul-up".

Bleach, who diplomats said served with the British army in Northern Ireland and later ran a defence sales business in Yorkshire, has said he was acting as the "inside man" for the British government in the arms drop. Britain denies the claim.

Diplomats have said Britain tipped off India before the arms drop. But the report said the Indian Home Ministry, despite intelligence information it had received, did not alert all other concerned agencies.
The Civil Aviation Ministry did not check the aircraft when it landed in the northern city of Varanasi before the arms drop, and failed to seek air defence clearance for the plane, it said.
The Defence Ministry cleared the plane's flight between Madras and Karachi four days after the drop even though it suspected the aircraft may have dropped the arms, it said.
The report said the ministries had shown "uncanny skill in blaming each other".

"The fact is that a foreign aircraft loaded with sophisticated arms flew into the Indian skies, halted at a few places, dropped arms at a place while flying between two stations, went out of India and came back to India after two days and remained in the country for a day without being detected," it said.
It said the panel accepted "the frank admission by the home secretary that there was a total failure on the part of the government agencies".
